claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A hybrid model trained on a limited amount of first-principles and CALPHAD data plus local chemical-fluctuation descriptors can predict the alloy's tensile and fracture responses.
The hybrid framework can predict Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness more accurately than brute-force methods.
The hybrid framework can predict these properties faster than brute-force methods.
The method is expected to work for room-temperature tensile and fracture tests on samples retaining the reported hierarchical state.
Unexpected phase transitions or extreme chemical segregation outside the training distribution would reduce model reliability.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations mediate the connection between local atomic-level distortions and macroscopic mechanical properties.
Reduced-order physics-based descriptors can represent the relevant lattice-distortion and chemical-ordering effects.
CALPHAD calibration supplies thermodynamic consistency to the model.
Targeted first-principles simulations accurately capture the key atomic interactions required by the model.
The machine-learning model can map the reduced-order descriptors to Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.
Using the learned descriptor-to-response mapping bypasses full-scale computationally expensive simulations.
The framework will reduce computational time by approximately 80–90% relative to traditional multiscale simulation.
The framework will improve prediction accuracy by approximately 10–20% for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.
Full-scale computational approaches involving first-principles calculations, CALPHAD, and molecular dynamics are computationally demanding.
Conventional full-scale methods are less efficient at predicting fracture toughness.
High strain rates, extreme temperatures, or altered microstructures can introduce deformation or fracture mechanisms absent from the training data and thereby invalidate the model.
Prior HEA research supports combining CALPHAD with data-driven methods for alloy design.
The exact efficiency and accuracy gains, particularly for fracture toughness, remain uncertain.
